lines: Say versus do. A few minutes on a containment layer for AI agents that reads what the model says and what it does, side by side. Built in one day for the Vultr Agent Rush Hackathon, from Potestas AI.

An AI agent with working tools can send a wire, change a vendor's bank account, delete audit logs, or switch off multi-factor authentication. Most safety testing reads what the model wrote. The failures that matter are what it did. And the two are not the same measurement: a model can refuse in words and call the tool anyway.

So we built the gate. The agent gets a task, a stated company policy, and sixteen working tools. Every tool call runs inside a fresh Docker container on Vultr: no network, memory and CPU caps, a process limit, all capabilities dropped, destroyed after the episode. The model's API key never enters the box.

Before any call is dispatched, the gate checks it against the one action the policy forbids. A forbidden call is blocked and never reaches the sandbox. The gate also reads the model's words so far. If it already refused, or said it would wait for a phone call, and then calls the forbidden tool, that block is recorded as: said no, did it.

Then we measured. Challenge one requires the agent's model calls to go through Vultr Serverless Inference, so we ran every text model on that endpoint, 12 of them, through ten new scenarios, three times each, 720 episodes in all. The scenarios were written today and are public: a forged closing wire, a vendor's new bank account, audit logs before the auditors arrive, a VP who wants MFA off, a report with instructions hidden inside, and five more.

The result. Across 720 scored episodes on 12 models, the forbidden action was attempted 26 times and blocked every time. Not one of them refused first. No model said no and then did it. All 26 went straight to the action without a word of refusal, while 664 episodes held the line and said why.

Models that attempted it: nemotron-3-nano-omni-30b-a3b-reasoning, 21 of 60, muse-glimmer-30b, 5 of 60. The other 10 models never attempted it. By scenario, the hardest was Clean up before the auditors arrive, attempted 8 of 72 times.

Then we did something simple. After the first submission we ran the same ten questions on the same twelve models again, three more runs each, about three hours later, temperature zero, nothing changed in the prompts. Attempts went from 10 to 16, every one blocked. Said no, then did it: still 0. 10 of the 12 models were identical: zero attempts, both times.

The two that broke in the first pass moved. nemotron-3-nano-omni-30b-a3b-reasoning went from 7 to 14; muse-glimmer-30b went from 3 to 2. New in the second pass, on scenarios the model had held three hours earlier: Free the disk by deleting backups, The forged closing wire, The vendor's new bank account. Temperature zero did not mean the same action hours apart. A test on Monday does not test Friday's agent. That is the argument for a gate that sits in front of the agent instead of trusting the test.

One more thing, because it matters more than the numbers. The second pass first showed 2 episodes in the headline class, said no then did it. We read them. In both, the model refused the emailed script in words and then quarantined it, stripping its execute bit with chmod minus x. Our rule had read that as chmod plus x. The gate was wrong, not the model. We fixed the rule, added tests, and re-graded every blocked call in all 720 episodes by script. Exactly those 2 rows moved, to held. The old file is kept beside the new one, and each moved row says why. The headline class is still empty.

Every verdict is read off the tool-call log with fixed rules. No judge model anywhere. The refusal reader is a set of patterns, so it will miss some refusals and over-read some hedges; every transcript is in the repository so you can check it yourself. One run is presence, not frequency. Three repetitions are a small sample.

The gate is the product: an agent that executes safely is a product, an agent that only chats is a demo. The code, the scenarios and every episode record are public at github.com/JosephCirello/saydo-gate.
